text: Did the student lose course places because someone else or an automated system grabbed them first?
Did the student herself accidentally remove or drop all her enrolled courses?
Did the student have her course selections saved in a shopping cart or draft that expired or was cleared without being submitted?
Did the student miss the course-selection deadline entirely because she was unaware of the correct deadline?
Was the student unable to access the course-selection system that evening for a technical reason (such as a system crash, outage, or login problem)?
Did the student intentionally give up or trade away her courses to other students?
Did the student choose her courses but then fail to pay the tuition or course fees by the deadline, causing the enrollments to be cancelled?
Did the student's courses disappear because her student status or enrollment eligibility was revoked (for example, she was deregistered or had a hold placed on her account)?
Were the courses she wanted actually cancelled or removed by the university (rather than being taken by others or lost by her)?
Did the student misunderstand the course catalog or course codes and thus select wrong courses that were then automatically dropped?
Did the student's courses vanish because she (or her account) was logged in simultaneously on multiple devices, causing a session conflict that reverted her selections?
Did the student's courses disappear because of a time-zone confusion—she thought the deadline was at a different local time than the system used?
Is the "one evening" significant because the student was asleep or otherwise unconscious/incapacitated during that evening?
Is the puzzle hinging on a wordplay or redefinition of "course" (for example, "courses" meaning dishes in a meal rather than academic classes)?
Does "all of my courses" refer to dishes served during a meal that evening?
Was the student dining in a university catered hall or dining event where all the courses were eaten or cleared away by others?
Did the student arrive late to the dining event, so that by the time she got there all the food courses had already been served and cleared?
Were the courses taken away because the student herself had to leave the dining event early (before the food was served)?
Did the student not actually get to eat the courses because she was busy serving them to others (as a server/volunteer at the dining event)?
Were the courses eaten by others because the student was the one who had prepared/cooked them and gave them all away to guests?
Did the food courses disappear from the student's table because the student was seated at the wrong table or in a different location from where the meal was served?
Did the student eat all the courses herself that evening, so they were "gone" because she consumed them?
Were the courses gone because the student was unable to eat them due to a dietary restriction or allergy, so her portions were given to or eaten by others?
Was the dining event a communal meal (like a hall dinner or hotpot) where dishes are shared at the table, and other diners ate all the courses before the student could take her share?
Did the student get distracted or pulled away from the table (e.g., by a phone call or task) so that while she was away, others finished all the courses?
Were the courses gone because the university dining hall ran out of food that evening (a shortage), so she was left without any courses?
Were the courses gone because the student's meal was shared with guests she had invited, who ate the food?
Was the disappearance of the courses connected to the student being in a university hall or residential college with a formal dinner (high table) tradition?
At this formal high-table dinner, was the student in a role or position that required her to stand, serve, or otherwise not eat with the diners (such as a student waiter)?

In the high-table tradition, do the diners stand up (e.g., when the high table party enters or leaves, or for a toast/grace), and each time they sit back down the courses/plates have been cleared away?

Was the student at a high-table dinner where she was seated at a table that was not actually being served the courses (e.g., a side table, or a seat added outside the main seating), so the courses never came to her?
Was the student's "course selection" in the puzzle actually her choosing which dishes/courses she would eat at the high-table dinner—and those chosen courses were all taken by others?

Did the student choose her courses (dishes) but then fail to secure them because another diner at the high table was served her portions before her—i.e., a mix-up in which her chosen dishes went to someone else?

Was the dinner a self-service or order-in-advance system where the student's chosen dishes were all claimed by other diners before she reached the front, because she was slow or at the back of the queue?
Did the student herself not attend the high-table dinner, so others at the dinner ate the courses she had selected for herself?
Did the student's chosen courses get eaten by others while she was still selecting them—that is, she was choosing dishes from a shared selection and other diners took them all as she picked?
Is the "deadline" in the opening also part of the wordplay—referring to a deadline for choosing dinner courses rather than an academic course-registration deadline?

Was this a "course selection" event where the student had to choose her dinner courses by a deadline—and by the time she chose, other diners had already selected/claimed all the available courses/dishes, leaving nothing for her?

Did the student choose her dinner courses correctly by the deadline, but then the caterer/server mistakenly served her chosen courses to the other diners, so they were all gone by the time her turn came?
Was the student unable to eat her chosen courses because she was fasting (for religious or health reasons) that evening, so others ate them?
Did the student's chosen courses go to waste or get eaten because the dinner was cancelled or she was told not to come, so the food she had chosen was served to others instead?
Were the courses she chose collectively a set of dishes to be shared at her table, which the other diners at her table consumed entirely before she could eat any?
Did the student choose the courses as her contribution to a potluck/communal dinner, and other people ate them all—so "her courses" were gone?
During the dinner, was the student at the podium or otherwise performing/giving a speech each time the courses were served, so her food was served and cleared while she was away from her seat?
Was the student a guest at the high table who chose courses from the menu, but her food was cleared away uneaten because she was a vegetarian/didn't eat that dish and the waiters removed her plate?
Did the student's chosen courses disappear because the dinner was a themed/tasting event where each course was placed on a shared rotating table (lazy Susan) and other diners took her portions?
Was the student's chosen set of courses actually a "menu" she designed/selected for the whole dinner event (as an organizer), and the diners ate all of it, so nothing was left for her personally?
Was the student's seat at the high-table dinner occupied by another person (e.g., a substitute/guest who took her place), who then ate the courses that had been chosen/served for her?

Was the student's chosen-courses list submitted to the caterer/dining service, but the dinner actually held was a different night than the one she ordered for, so her chosen courses were served at the wrong dinner?

Did the student's chosen courses get eaten by others because, at the high-table dinner, the food is first presented/paraded and then carved/served by the high-table guests or officers—so the student's portions were distributed to the diners rather than kept for her?
Is the key point that the student is a student of food/cooking (like a culinary student), so "her courses" were dishes she prepared as coursework and they were eaten by others at the dinner?
Were the "courses" chosen for a wedding/banquet held in the hall, and the dishes were shared/cleared as part of the celebration, leaving the student without her chosen portions?

Did the student's chosen courses get eaten by the other diners because the dinner was served "family style" and her pre-chosen dishes were placed on the table before she arrived at the table, and finished by others in the meantime?

At the formal dinner, was each course cleared away as soon as the high-table party finished that course, so the student—eating more slowly—had her remaining chosen courses removed before she could finish them?
Was the food (the chosen courses) delivered to the student's hall/room, and other residents/hallmates ate the delivered food before she got to it?
Did the student actually get to eat any of her chosen courses that evening, or were they all gone before/without her eating them?
Did the student actually eat at least some of her chosen courses that evening?
Were the courses she chose intended to be taken away or kept for later (e.g., extra portions/leftovers), rather than all eaten at the dinner itself?
Was the student responsible for providing/supplying the courses to the dinner (e.g., she brought or funded the food for the event), so once the diners ate them, "her courses" were all gone?

Were the courses cleared away course-by-course as the dinner program moved on (each next course replacing the previous), so that the student, eating slowly, found each of her courses gone before she could finish them?
Did another person deliberately take or steal the student's chosen courses/portions to eat them?
Were the courses she chose ingredients or food supplies she had stored/kept for herself, which were used up by others in preparing or serving the dinner that evening?
Were the student's chosen courses discarded or thrown away (e.g., as waste) rather than eaten by other people?

Were the student's chosen courses thrown away because the dinner was interrupted or ended early (for example, an emergency, fire alarm, or the hall closing), causing the food to be cleared and discarded?
Was the student choosing the dinner courses by tasting samples, so each chosen course was only a small sample that was tasted and then discarded—leaving her without a full meal?
Were her remaining courses on her plate cleared and discarded by waiters before she had finished, so the unfinished chosen courses were thrown away that evening?
Was the student repeatedly away from eating her courses (for example, busy talking, working, or serving others) so that waiters cleared her unfinished plates, treating her as done?
At the dinner, were the dishes actually served different from the specific courses the student had chosen—so the courses she selected were not served to her at all?
Were the courses served in such rapid succession (or with so little time between them) that the student had no chance to finish each course before the next arrived and the previous was cleared?
Were all the plates, including the student's unfinished courses, cleared and discarded at a set time because the dinner had a fixed end time or the venue had to close/be reset?
At the high-table dinner, were the plates cleared during a toast or ceremony (when diners stand), so that the student's unfinished courses were removed then?
Was the person who cleared/discarded the student's courses a member of the catering/serving staff (a waiter), as opposed to another diner?
Did she return or reject her courses as unsatisfactory (e.g., cold, wrong, or not as ordered), causing the waiter to take them away and discard them?
Did she reject every one of her chosen courses for the same reason (e.g., they were all cold or all wrong), so that each course was discarded and she ended the evening with none?
Was the reason she rejected all her courses that they were served cold (not at the proper temperature)?
Was the reason she rejected all her courses that the food was spoiled or gone off (unsafe to eat)?
Was the reason she rejected all her courses that they were not the dishes she had ordered (the kitchen sent the wrong dishes every time)?
Was the reason she rejected all her courses that they were too spicy or otherwise too strongly flavored/inedible for her taste?

Was the reason she rejected the courses something wrong with the food itself (a physical defect such as contamination, a foreign object, or it being undercooked), rather than an external rule or her own dietary choice?

Were all the courses taken back and discarded because of an official order affecting the whole dinner (such as a health/safety recall or the caterer being shut down), rather than anything specific to the student?
Were the courses rejected because they contained alcohol and the student was under the legal age to be served alcohol, so they had to be taken back and discarded?
Were the courses taken back and discarded because the student turned out not to be entitled to attend/eat at that dinner (for example, she was not a registered or eligible guest)?
Were the courses sent back and discarded because the student could not afford them (a price/billing issue) rather than for taste or dietary reasons?
Was the reason the courses were rejected a personal instruction or advice given to the student by a specific individual (such as a doctor, warden, or companion), rather than an institutional rule?
Was the institutional rule that caused the courses to be removed a hall tradition applying to first-year/freshman students at the high-table dinner?
Were the courses removed because they were not covered/authorized under the student's meal plan or dining account (a billing/entitlement rule of the university dining system)?

Were the courses all removed because they violated a religious dietary requirement observed for that dinner (for example, meat served on a day of religious abstinence, or non-halal food at a halal dinner)?
Were the courses discarded because of an institutional food-safety or hygiene rule (for example, food that had been out past a safe time had to be thrown away)?
Did the student's hall or dining membership end (or was it invalid that evening), so her courses could not be served to her and were removed?

Was the reason she could not finish and the courses were removed that she was physically unable to eat that evening (for example, due to recent dental work, illness, or a medical condition), so the waiter took the dishes away?
Was the reason she rejected/declined the courses simply that she was already full or no longer hungry, so the remaining dishes were taken away and discarded?
Did the waiter clear her courses prematurely because she had placed her cutlery (knife and fork) together in the "I've finished" position, mis-signaling that she was done?
Was the waiter's removal of her unfinished courses a simple mistake or misjudgment by the waiter, rather than following a policy or rule?

Was there a policy that each plate must be cleared after a fixed time limit (a set eating window per course), so the student's unfinished dishes were removed by rule regardless of whether she was done?
Had the student stored the courses (as pre-chosen/prepared food) in a shared hall fridge, which was cleared out and the food discarded by staff under the hall's fridge-cleaning policy?

Under the dinner's service policy, was each of the student's plates cleared as soon as the following course was brought out (standard banquet service), so any unfinished course was removed and discarded?
Were the courses part of a ritual offering (e.g., offered to ancestors, deities, or a hall patron) and then, by custom/policy, cleared and discarded rather than eaten?
Did the student eat any portion of the specific chosen dishes (the courses she selected), as opposed to only incidental food like bread, rice, or water served alongside?
Did the waiters clear the table (including her unfinished courses) because a principal or guest of honor finished or left the dinner, triggering the clearing of everyone's plates as policy?

The opening is a wordplay trap. "Courses" and the "deadline" do not refer to academic modules and course registration at all; they refer to the dishes (courses of a meal) that the student had to choose in advance for a university hall/high-table dinner. She is a student at HKU and did make her menu choices by the dinner deadline, but the puzzle is about the meal, not her degree.

At the formal hall dinner, the dishes she had chosen were served to her, but she managed only to taste a small portion of each one. Her plates were then cleared by the waiting staff before she had finished, and the unfinished food was taken away and thrown out rather than kept for her. Because the dishes had been removed and discarded, by the end of the evening all the courses she had chosen were "gone," leaving her without a full dinner even though nothing supernatural or academic had happened.
